doc.title: Bernie Kirsh interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 27, 2022

chapter: Patti Smith and Return to Forever recordings
title: Recording Leprechaun live in the room and mixing by hand
summary: Strings, horns, rhythm section and vocalist in one room, John Storyk's room, and hands-on-faders mixing with limited tracks.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: As an engineer to go from Patti Smith to that “Leprechaun” it seems to me to be quite a leap because you had to record strings and woodwinds and vocals, so —

Yeah well they were all live in the room too. I mean it was all in one room. We had — I had the string quartet in one area, the horns in another, the rhythm section, two bass players, you know, piano and Gayle’s in the booth singing. So there’s a lot of activity which added to fun factor the minute it went out the roof, having all those musicians on the room.
Did the room have a distinct sound itself?

I don’t know that it did. I think it allowed for what was recorded in there to sound pleasant and musical. You know you wouldn’t get sounds occurring in another part of the room that weren’t favorable coming in. The room was set up nicely acoustically. John Storyk was the architect and I think it was his first studio by the way too. I think. I may be wrong, but I think so. And anyway so we have a roomful of musicians and you know we have Steve Gadd sitting in, it wasn’t a drum booth but it was like a partition that went around the drums and he had three or four music stands in front of him with the music strewn like this and he’d be reading the music and playing. And it was just that. It was just a busy scene of competence showing itself off.
And Chick arranged all that music himself?

He did, yeah. And great musicians. So that was — and that project was exactly what I understood. I understood from a mixer’s point of view what that music was. It was just very real to me. I didn’t have — nothing to think about. I could just set up things and do what I needed to do to get the final result. So it wasn’t a lot of trial and error going on. It © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

was, oh I heard that and I’d try to accomplish that, and it just went on. I mean of course with Chick’s music you can’t go far afield anyway from anything that sounds great because what you’re working with lends itself easily to enjoyment. I don’t think you can mess it up too much.
Were the mixes done with just Chick and yourself?
Yeah. Just hands on the faders. You know there was no automation in those days.
Oh right. Hands on faders. Yeah.

Hands on faders. So you know mostly it would just be he would, I guess from time to time he would come in and handle something but mostly it was just my own figuring it out, how to accomplish it. I mean it was recorded in a way that it wasn’t a lot of crazy moves to do and that sort of thing. But what we did have of course were, you only have a certain amount of tracks. So if you’re doing overdubs you have to share tracks with something that’s already recorded on one portion. So you’d have maybe — not that this was the case — but let’s say you had I don’t know a keyboard playing on the verses but not on the choruses. So you could use the choruses for something else. So you’d record another instrument on that track in the space where you had the chorus. And you know then you’d have to deal with that fader.
